title: Half the subnet cannot reach the new server
tagline: A server was renumbered after a migration. Hosts below .128 reach it; hosts above .128 do not. The mask is the villain.
environment: Access switch with one flat VLAN
40 workstations in the same physical segment
topology:
workstations 10.0.20.10-.240 --[access switch, VLAN 20]--> gateway 10.0.20.1
server 10.0.20.130/25 on the same switch
symptoms: Workstations with addresses below 10.0.20.128 can reach the server
The server can ping 10.0.20.11 but not 10.0.20.1
Nothing is logged on the switch, and the port shows no errors
objectives: Read the mask, not just the address, in ip output
Compute the subnet and broadcast for a given prefix length
Explain why a wrong mask produces a partial, address-dependent failure
framework: Which hosts fail and is there a pattern in their addresses?
What does the failing host think its own subnet is?
Is the gateway considered on-link by that host?

evidence.label: The server's own addressing
evidence.command: ip -brief address show dev eth0; ip route
evidence.output:
eth0  UP  10.0.20.130/25

10.0.20.128/25 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.20.130
evidence.insight: The prefix is /25, so the server believes its subnet is 10.0.20.128-10.0.20.255 and its gateway 10.0.20.1 is off-link. Every other host on this segment uses /24.

evidence.label: What a working host uses
evidence.command: ip -brief address show dev eth0; ip route | head -3
evidence.output:
eth0  UP  10.0.20.11/24

default via 10.0.20.1 dev eth0 proto static
10.0.20.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.20.11
evidence.insight: Working hosts use /24 with the gateway on-link. The mismatch between /25 and /24 is the entire defect: two different ideas of where the subnet ends.

evidence.label: Test from the server to a low and a high address
evidence.output:
PING 10.0.20.11 (10.0.20.11) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.0.20.11: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.412 ms
---
PING 10.0.20.200 (10.0.20.200) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.0.20.130 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
evidence.insight: 10.0.20.11 is inside 10.0.20.128/25? No — and yet it works, because the server ARPs and gets an answer on the shared segment. 10.0.20.200 fails with ARP-level unreachability, showing it is a Layer 2 adjacency judgement, not a routing failure.

evidence.label: The gateway test that decides it
evidence.output:
From 10.0.20.130 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable

203.0.113.20 via 10.0.20.1 dev eth0 src 10.0.20.130 uid 1000
    cache
    (no route error, but ARP for 10.0.20.1 will fail)
evidence.insight: The server thinks the gateway is a directly reachable neighbour and ARPs for it. No host owns 10.0.20.1 in the 10.0.20.128/25 range, so ARP fails and everything off-link dies.

evidence.label: Confirm with a neighbour table
evidence.insight: FAILED entries prove the server is trying to reach these addresses directly on the wire and nobody answers. A router would have replied; here there is no router because the mask excludes one.

evidence.label: Watch the ARP attempts
evidence.command: sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 arp and host 10.0.20.1 -c4
evidence.output:
10:31:02.101 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.20.1 tell 10.0.20.130, length 28
10:31:03.108 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.20.1 tell 10.0.20.130, length 28
10:31:04.115 ARP, Request who-has 10.0.20.1 tell 10.0.20.130, length 28
evidence.insight: Repeated ARP requests for the gateway with no reply. The server is not routing; it is shouting on the local segment for an address that lives on another subnet.

hypotheses.text: The switch has a MAC table problem affecting some addresses.
hypotheses.why: Which hosts fail correlates exactly with address ranges, not with ports, and the switch reports no errors.

hypotheses.text: The server's subnet mask is /25 instead of /24, so it misjudges which addresses are on-link.
hypotheses.why: eth0 is 10.0.20.130/25, the gateway is outside that range, and ARP for 10.0.20.1 and 10.0.20.200 never resolves.

hypotheses.text: A firewall is blocking traffic between address ranges.
hypotheses.why: The failures happen at ARP resolution, before any firewall could evaluate a packet.
A default route exists; it is unusable because its next hop is wrongly considered on-link.

solution.root_cause: The server was configured with 10.0.20.130/25 instead of 10.0.20.130/24. Its own subnet is therefore 10.0.20.128-255, which places the gateway 10.0.20.1 and the lower half of the segment outside its subnet. The server ARPs for those addresses directly on the wire, nobody answers, and every off-link flow fails with 'Destination Host Unreachable'.
solution.resolution: Correct the prefix to /24 so the connected route becomes 10.0.20.0/24 and the gateway is treated as an on-link next hop. With NetworkManager use nmcli con modify <con> ipv4.addresses 10.0.20.130/24 and reactivate, rather than editing a file that a profile may overwrite.
solution.verification: ip route shows 10.0.20.0/24 as the connected route; ip route get 203.0.113.20 resolves via 10.0.20.1; ping to the gateway and to a host above .128 both succeed; and hosts in both halves of the segment reach the server. Confirm from the other direction too, not only from the server.
lessons: An address without a mask is half a fact. Always read the prefix.
Address-dependent failures usually mean an on-link/off-link disagreement, not a policy.
FAILED neighbour entries localise the problem to Layer 2 adjacency in one command.
interview_followups: What is the broadcast address of 10.0.20.130/25, and of /24?
How does the host decide whether to ARP for a destination or send to the gateway?
Why did some hosts still work, even though the server's mask was wrong?

resolution_options.text: Change the server's prefix from /25 to /24
resolution_options.why: Restores the intended connected route and makes the gateway an on-link next hop again.

resolution_options.text: Add a static route for 10.0.20.0/24 via 10.0.20.1
resolution_options.why: The address is inside that subnet anyway, so the local /25 route still wins; it does not fix the on-link judgement.

resolution_options.text: Ask the network team to move all hosts into 10.0.20.128/25
resolution_options.why: Renumbering 40 hosts to accommodate one wrong mask inverts the cost.
A workaround at the wrong layer that leaves the configuration error in place.
The configuration is persistent; a reboot reproduces the same state.

interview_questions.q: How does a host decide whether to ARP for a destination?
interview_questions.a: It applies its own mask to the destination. If the result equals its own network, the destination is on-link and it ARPs directly. Otherwise it ARPs for the gateway. A wrong mask therefore changes the decision itself, not just the routing table.

interview_questions.q: A host can ping some machines but not others in 'the same subnet'. What do you check first?
interview_questions.a: The mask on both ends and the resulting connected route. Then ip neigh to see whether ARP is failing, which proves the on-link judgement is wrong.

interview_questions.q: Why can a wrong mask still allow partial communication?
interview_questions.a: The shared Layer 2 segment does not care about masks: if the sender ARPs and the target answers, traffic flows. So only addresses that the mask classifies as off-link break, producing an address-dependent pattern.
